model_b.text:
**Objective** To establish a hyperuricemia rat model using potassium oxonate and yeast, and investigate the intervention effect and mechanism of sulforaphane on hyperuricemic rats based on urine metabolomics.  

**Methods** Forty male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats (6–8 weeks old, weighing 180–220 g) were randomly divided into four groups: blank control group, hyperuricemia group, allopurinol group (intervened with 10 mg/kg·bw allopurinol), and sulforaphane group (intervened with 10 mg/kg·bw glucoraphanin + myrosinase). The blank control and hyperuricemia groups were administered distilled water by gavage. After six weeks of experimental intervention, serum uric acid (SUA), liver and kidney function indices, renal histopathology, and urine metabolomics were analyzed.  

**Results**  
(1) Compared with the blank control group, the hyperuricemia group showed significantly increased SUA, urinary uric acid (UUA), urinary creatinine (UCr), and creatinine clearance (CCr), along with decreased uric acid clearance (CUA), with statistical significance (P < 0.05), indicating successful model establishment. Urine metabolomics revealed eight signature differential metabolites in the hyperuricemia group compared to the blank control group: myo-inositol (upregulated via galactose metabolism), uracil (upregulated via β-alanine metabolism), γ-aminobutyric acid (upregulated via arginine and proline metabolism), valine (upregulated via pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis), and galactose and mannose (downregulated via galactose metabolism), as well as threonic acid and D-gluconic acid (downregulated via ascorbate and aldarate metabolism).  

(2) After six weeks of intervention, compared with the hyperuricemia group, the sulforaphane group exhibited significantly reduced SUA, serum creatinine (SCr), and UCr levels (P < 0.05). Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) decreased, while the albumin/globulin (A/G) ratio increased, and total cholesterol (TC) was significantly reduced. Compared to the hyperuricemia group, the sulforaphane group exhibited seven key metabolic pathways and five signature differential metabolites, including amino acid biosynthesis and metabolism, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (with downregulated 4-hydroxyproline and proline, and upregulated succinate and α-ketoglutarate), and the ascorbate and aldarate metabolism pathway (with upregulated threonic acid).  

**Conclusion** Sulforaphane primarily reduces uric acid levels by influencing uric acid excretion. The mechanism may involve modulating lysine degradation, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, starch and sucrose metabolism pathways, enhancing antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capacity, reducing oxidative stress, improving energy metabolism disorders and renal dysfunction, thereby mitigating hyperuricemia-induced kidney damage and enhancing renal uric acid excretion. Ultimately, sulforaphane demonstrates potential for preventing and treating hyperuricemia.
